stem: Which is an internal parasite of livestock?

options.content: Liver fluke
options.rationale: Correct: lives in the bile ducts.

options.content: Blue tick
Louse
Mange mite
options.rationale: An external parasite of the skin.

explanation: Liver fluke lives inside the liver; ticks, lice and mites live on the skin.

stem: Which organism is the intermediate host of the liver fluke?

options.content: A water snail
The tsetse fly
The earthworm
options.rationale: Not part of the fluke's life cycle.

options.content: A pasture tick
options.rationale: Ticks are not hosts of liver fluke.

explanation: Fluke larvae multiply inside water snails before forming cysts on grass.

stem: In the life cycle of a roundworm of sheep, which stage is swallowed by the sheep?

options.content: The adult worm in the dung
The infective larva on the grass
The egg inside a water snail
A cyst in the muscle of a pig

explanation: Eggs hatch in dung; larvae moult to the infective stage, climb grass and are eaten.

stem: A goat has pale inner eyelids and a soft swelling under the jaw. Which parasite is most likely responsible?

options.content: Brown ear tick
options.rationale: Attaches in the ears; not linked to bottle jaw.

options.content: Mange mite
Wireworm, a blood-sucking roundworm
Tapeworm segments in the small intestine
options.rationale: Tapeworms do not usually cause severe anaemia.

explanation: Wireworm sucks blood in the abomasum, causing anaemia and fluid under the jaw (bottle jaw).
hints: Bottle jaw follows loss of blood protein.

stem: Why should a group of animals be dosed according to the weight of the heaviest animal?

options.content: Because heavier animals always carry the most worms
To avoid under-dosing that leaves worms alive
To use up the drug faster
Light animals need no dewormer

explanation: Under-dosed worms survive and their offspring are more likely to be resistant to the drug.
hints: What happens to worms that receive too little drug?

stem: Why are worm burdens usually highest in the rainy season?

options.content: Animals drink less water when it rains
options.rationale: Drinking has little effect on worms.

options.content: Dewormers do not work properly in wet, rainy weather
Worms die in dry dung, so dung is not passed
Warm, moist weather helps larvae develop
options.rationale: Correct: larvae also climb wet grass.

explanation: Eggs hatch and larvae develop fast in warm, wet weather and move up wet grass, so infection peaks in the rains.
hints: What do larvae need to survive and move?

stem: Which measure best breaks the life cycle of the beef tapeworm?

options.content: Dosing all the cattle with a dewormer every single week
options.rationale: Cysts in muscle are not the target.

options.content: Using toilets so human faeces do not reach grazing
Draining swamps to kill water snails
Dipping cattle in acaricide

explanation: The adult lives in people; cattle are infected by eggs from human faeces, so sanitation (with meat inspection and thorough cooking) breaks the cycle.
hints: Where does the adult beef tapeworm live?

options.content: A chemical that kills ticks
A vaccine against worms
A feed that fattens wormy animals
A drug that kills internal worms

stem: Roundworms of sheep and goats have a direct life cycle with no intermediate host.
explanation: True. Larvae develop on pasture and are swallowed by the same kind of host.

stem: Match each parasite with a feature.
explanation: Learn the body shape and life cycle feature of each group.

payload.template: Adults in gut → eggs passed in {{blank:a}} → larvae develop on pasture → infective larvae climb {{blank:b}} → swallowed by grazing animal.

explanation: Eggs leave in dung; infective larvae move up grass blades.

stem: Name the swelling under the jaw of sheep and goats caused by fluid collecting when worms cause loss of blood protein.
Assume a dewormer is given at 2.5 mL per 10 kg body weight. The heaviest sheep in a group weighs 48 kg. Calculate the dose for each sheep, in mL.
A farmer checks 36 goats with an eyelid colour chart and finds 9 very pale. Calculate the percentage that are anaemic.
Dosed lambs gain 160 g a day and undosed lambs on the same pasture gain 110 g a day. Calculate the extra live mass, in kg, that each dosed lamb gains over 90 days.
workedSolution:
1. Extra gain per day = 160 − 110 = 50 g.
2. Over 90 days = 50 × 90 = 4,500 g.
3. 4,500 ÷ 1,000 = 4.5 kg per lamb.
hints: Extra gain per day × days, then convert g to kg.

stem: Describe **four** signs that a herd of young cattle has a heavy burden of internal worms.

points.description: Loss of weight / poor growth despite enough feed.
Diarrhoea and dirty hindquarters / pot belly / worms or segments in dung / coughing.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The calves grow poorly and lose condition although feed is good, their coats are rough and dull, their eye membranes are pale, and they have diarrhoea with dirty hindquarters.

stem: Explain how draining a swampy area of a farm helps to control liver fluke.

points.description: Water snails, the intermediate hosts, live in wet, swampy areas.
Without water the snails die / cannot breed, so fluke larvae cannot multiply.
Fewer cysts form on grass at the water's edge, so fewer are swallowed by grazing animals.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The fluke must pass through water snails, which live in swamps. Draining removes the snails' habitat, so the larvae cannot multiply and fewer cysts form on the grass that cattle eat.

explanation: Break the cycle at the intermediate host.

stem:
A school near Gweru compared two groups of weaned kids over 12 weeks of the rainy season. Both groups were dewormed at the start.

| Grazing system | Kids | Mean gain over 12 weeks (kg) | Kids with bottle jaw |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same paddock all season | 12 | 3.1 | 7 |
| Rotated through 4 paddocks | 12 | 4.6 | 1 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the difference in mean gain between the two groups, in kg.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the rotated kids' extra gain as a percentage of the gain of the kids kept in one paddock, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean daily gain of the rotated kids, in g/day, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why the kids kept in one paddock all season grew less and had more bottle jaw.

points.description: Dung from the kids built up eggs and larvae on the single paddock all season.
Warm, wet weather let many larvae reach the infective stage on the grass, so the kids were constantly reinfected (after the first dose).
Blood-sucking worms caused anaemia and protein loss (bottle jaw), so less feed went to growth; rotation rested paddocks so larvae died.

explanation: Analyse a grazing trial and link worm control to the roundworm life cycle.
hints: How does rotation affect larvae on the grass?

stem: Several cattle on a farm near Marondera are thin and anaemic. Leaf-shaped flat worms are found in the bile ducts of a cow slaughtered on the farm. The cattle drink from a marshy stream with many small snails.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: What is the role of the snails?

options.content: They eat the fluke eggs and destroy them
options.rationale: They do not control the fluke.

options.content: They are the final host of the adult fluke
options.rationale: The cattle are the final host.

options.content: They are the intermediate host
options.rationale: Correct: the larvae multiply inside them.

options.content: They carry ticks to the cattle

parts.explanation: The snail is the intermediate host in which fluke larvae multiply.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the cattle become infected.

points.description: Larvae leaving the snails form cysts on grass at the water's edge.
Cattle grazing or drinking at the marsh swallow the cysts; young flukes migrate through the liver to the bile ducts.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **two** ways of controlling the fluke on this farm.

points.description: Fence off the marsh and provide water from troughs / drain the marsh.
Dose the cattle with a drug that kills flukes / control the snails.

explanation: Identify liver fluke and plan control through its life cycle.
hints: Which parasite is leaf-shaped and lives in the bile ducts?
